title: Connexions de Gauss-Manin et équations de Picard-Fuchs. Opération de Cartier : copies de tapuscrit annoté (s.d.), tiré à part (1981), notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
This is page 18 of a typescript. It is the 'Formulaire' on elliptic curves in Weierstrass form, in the style of Tate. This matches Deligne's 'Courbes elliptiques : formulaire d'après J. Tate' (Modular Functions of One Variable IV, LNM 476, 1975). The surrounding numbering (1.6, 1.7, 3.1, 4.1, 4.3) and the earlier remark that a1 and ±b2 are the Hasse–Witt invariants also fit that text. The proposition number here (7.2) may differ from the printed version.

Modular forms are meant in Deligne–Katz style: rules f(E, ω) for elliptic curves with an invertible differential over any base of characteristic p, satisfying f(E, λ^{-1}ω) = λ^k f(E, ω). The page completes the claim that a mod-p relation among c4, c6, Δ is divisible by c4^3 − c6^2. It does so by determining the full graded ring of modular forms in characteristics 2 and 3.

(I) p = 2: the ring is F2[a1, Δ], with c4 = a1^4 and c6 = a1^6.
- Since b2 = a1^2 + 4a2 ≡ a1^2, we get c4 = b2^2 − 24b4 ≡ a1^4 and c6 = −b2^3 + 36b2b4 − 216b6 ≡ a1^6.
- a1 is a modular form of weight 1 = p − 1, the Hasse invariant; this follows from the transformation formulas (1.6), (1.7).
- Proof sketch, ordinary locus first. Where a1 is invertible, the curve can be written y^2 + a1xy = x^3 + a2x^2 + a6 with π = dx/(a1x).
- In this form a2 is defined only up to Artin–Schreier modification, so it is not an invariant. Forms are therefore a1^{-n}P(a1, a6) with P isobaric.
- Since Δ = a1^6 a6 in characteristic 2, these are the same as a1^{-m}Q(a1, Δ).
- Extension: such a form extends over the supersingular locus a1 = 0, Δ ≠ 0 (j = 0) iff it is a polynomial in a1 and Δ.

(II) p = 3: the ring is F3[b2, Δ], with c4 = b2^2 and c6 = −b2^3.
- b2 is the Hasse invariant of weight 2.
- On the locus where c4 is invertible, the curve can be put in the form d6 = 0, which is equivalent to a4 = 0 in (3.1). Forms are then b2^{-n}P(b2, Δ) (continued on the next page).
- Such a form extends to j = 0 iff it is polynomial in b2 and Δ.

As a consequence, c4^3 − c6^2 vanishes identically mod 2 and mod 3, consistent with c4^3 − c6^2 = 1728Δ. This gives the divisibility claim at the top of the page.
errors: No mathematical errors. The congruences c4 ≡ a1^4, c6 ≡ a1^6 (mod 2) and c4 ≡ b2^2, c6 ≡ −b2^3 (mod 3) check out from Tate's formulas.

The proof is a sketch with two gaps. First, it does not spell out why a form cannot depend on a2 in characteristic 2: a2 is only defined up to Artin–Schreier modification, and forms are étale-local. Second, the extension across the divisor a1 = 0 (resp. b2 = 0) is just 'absence of poles', which is not argued in detail.

ideas.what: Ring of mod-2 modular forms (Deligne–Katz sense, all weights) is F2[a1, Δ], with a1 the Hasse invariant of weight 1
ideas.modern_name: Graded ring of modular forms of level 1 in characteristic 2
ideas.usually_credited_to: Deligne, 'Formulaire' (LNM 476, 1975), after Tate; cf. Katz, 'p-adic properties of modular schemes and modular forms' (1973), and Serre / Swinnerton-Dyer on mod p modular forms
ideas.where_published: Deligne, Courbes elliptiques: formulaire d'après J. Tate, LNM 476 (1975)

ideas.what: Ring of mod-3 modular forms is F3[b2, Δ], with b2 the Hasse invariant of weight 2, c4 = b2^2, c6 = −b2^3
ideas.modern_name: Graded ring of modular forms of level 1 in characteristic 3

ideas.what: Method: compute forms on the ordinary locus via a normal form, then test extension over the supersingular point j = 0

deep.surprise_reason: The page appears to be a copy of Deligne's published Tate 'Formulaire' (Antwerp IV), kept in Grothendieck's file on Gauss–Manin and Cartier operations. Its content is standard and published.
transcription_corrections: The transcription matches the image. The image has a typing smudge ('C3s' for 'Ces'), which the transcription correctly renders as 'Ces'.
